title: Clinging
hookLine: holding on to God through the whole day

cards: A small child crossing a busy street holds a parent's hand. The child isn't thinking about the hand the whole time. They're chatting, pointing at a dog, counting buses.
But the hand never lets go. In Deuteronomy, Moses tells the people: "But ye that did cleave unto the LORD your God are alive every one of you this day." Cleave.
Hold fast. The Torah asks for it more than once. The rabbis, and later the Hasidic teachers, asked the obvious question: how does a person do that, all day long, in the middle of everything else?

teach.h: HOW DO YOU HOLD A FIRE?
teach.b: Devekut. Clinging, attachment, holding on to God. First, the problem.
The Torah tells the people to cleave to God. But the Talmud raises an objection. The Torah also describes God as a fire that consumes.
How can anyone hold on to a fire? Second, the rabbis' answers.
In one passage, the Talmud says: walk after God's ways. As God clothed the naked, clothe the naked. As God visited the sick, visit the sick.
As God comforted mourners and buried the dead, do the same. In another passage, the answer is to attach yourself to the wise, to stand close to people who live by the Torah and help them.

Either way, clinging to God turns into something your hands do. Third, the Hasidic turn. Hasidic teachers made devekut a center of the spiritual life, and they refused to keep it inside the synagogue.
Hold on to God while praying, yes, and also while eating, working, walking, talking with a neighbor. Yesterday's line, no place without God, is what makes that possible.
If God is in every place, then every place is somewhere to hold on. Fourth, the hand. Devekut doesn't ask a person to stop living and stare at heaven.
Like the child on the street, attention can wander to a dog or a bus while the hold stays firm. A hand can slip.

teach.h: WHEN THE HAND SLIPS, TAKE HOLD.
teach.b: The practice is to notice, and take hold again.
So clinging, in this tradition, is less like a grip of fear and more like walking with someone you trust, all the way across.

how: In Hasidic teaching, devekut is pursued in prayer and also in daily activities such as eating, work and conversation, while the Talmud's teaching to walk in God's ways is lived through acts like visiting the sick and comforting mourners.

o: clinging to God through prayer, kindness and daily work
a fear of God that keeps a person at a distance
a vow to leave ordinary life for full-time prayer

p: ye that did cleave … are alive
clothe the naked, visit the sick

s: the Talmud asks how a person could cling to God at all
the Torah describes God as a consuming fire; the rabbis look for a way to hold on.
in the Talmud, clinging to God means leaving ordinary life
it means walking in God's ways: clothing, visiting, comforting, burying.
Hasidic devekut is only for times of prayer
Hasidic teachers carried it into eating, working, walking and talking.

games.q: the Torah tells you to cleave to God, but it also calls God a consuming fire. how does the Talmud say you can hold on?
o: you can't: the command is only for angels.
walk in God's ways: clothe the naked, visit the sick, comfort mourners.
stay away from people and think only of God.
games.why: as God clothed the naked and visited the sick, the Talmud says, so you do the same: clinging becomes kindness.

practice: Choose a chore, washing a cup, folding a shirt, wiping a counter, and do it slowly now, or picture doing it.

As your hands work, keep one thread of attention on God, or, if that word doesn't fit you, on what you're grateful for, the way a hand is held crossing the street. When your mind wanders, come back to the thread.

wordCard.voice: Devekut. Clinging: holding on to God through the whole day, in prayer, in kindness and in ordinary work. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: cling. A hand can slip, and the practice is simply to take hold again. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: But ye that did cleave unto the LORD your God are alive every one of you this day.
